A straight forward oatmeal-based cookie. Some variations can be quite good.

1 and 1/2 cup of flour
1 teaspoon of baking powder
1 cup of brown sugar
2/3 cups of shortening
2 tablespoons of milk
1/2 teaspoon of baking soda
1 cup of oatmeal
1/4 cup of chocolate chips
1/4 cup of walnuts
2 eggs
a pinch of salt
a teaspoon of cinnamon
vanilla

aluminium foil
2 cookie sheets
a good cookie-lifting spatula

In a large bowl beat eggs lightly to break the yolks, then mix in the shortening of choice, butter is best.

The shortening/egg mixture should be loose, add the brown sugar. Once that is mixed add the remaining liquids, mix well then add the salt to the liquid mixture.

Mix the baking powder, soda, flour and oatmeal together in another bowl.

Blend the liquid and solid mixes together.

Stir in chocolate chips and chopped walnuts.

Make balls and place onto a aluminium foiled pan then into an oven heated to 180°C (350°F) and let bake for between 15-20 minutes, keep a close eye on them after the 10 minute mark. Once they hit brown they are done even if they don't seem that way, they will get more solid after around 10 minutes of cooling.

The best of the many variations of this cookie is to ditch the walnuts and chocolate chips, grab a jam of your choice. Press down the balls of cookie dough using a spoon to create a dip in the middle and glob a spoon full of your jam into it before you start cooking. Turns out awesome.

The game is called 1337h4x and it's an endless runner, of sorts, where you play as a hacker navigating his packets down the information superhighway, speeding past mainframes, attacking vulnerable hosts to grow your botnet, avoiding firewalls, and using exit nodes to reduce your visibility. The Ludum Dare themes this time (there were two) were two button controls and growth. You could do both themes or just one of them without voting penalty but I wanted to do both. I thought it was an interesting challenge and, really, it gave me ideas for the game's components.

http://ludumdare.com/compo/ludum-dare-34/?action=preview&uid=64982

This was submitted for the competition, which lasts 48 hours and requires that you create all your assets from scratch. I'm generally a programmer as my art skills are quite lacking, but I figured this was a good chance to at least try to make some art. I kept it simple and I think it works. There are a few things I'd like to change but just didn't have enough time for those refinements in the competition. I do think I'll grow this out to a full game, though, and I started working on some of those graphical improvements today.

The aesthetic is heavily inspired by the movie Hackers, which should be immediately obvious to anyone familiar with the Gibson. I have a background in information security and I've wanted to make a hacking game for a while. I thought this was as good a chance as any to do that and I'll have to say, I like what I did with it. I was able to keep it simple and that really helped to just get it done.

On that note, this was a really good learning experience for me. The idea for the game actually started off much more complicated than what it ended up being. I originally intended to have several different minigames that would represent different steps in the hacking process. I was conscious of the dreaded feature creep, though, and started stripping features until all I had was this. I think I'm going to look at my other projects and start doing the same. It's easier to have a complete game to which you can add features than trying to compile a bunch of features into a completed game... if that makes any sense.

I also discovered that I'm capable of making something that almost sounds like music! I made the background loop with LMMS, an open source sequencer that works a bit like Fruity Loops, never having used the program before and only having a general understanding of how Fruity Loops works. I had some samples laying around just from my asset hoarding habits and I used them plus the default library of sounds from LMMS to compose a 60 second loop of driving techno that actually fits the game pretty well, I think. I've gotten compliments on it, so I'll take that as a personal victory. I don't know that I'd have ever really been as successful with creating music like that if I wasn't under the time constraints of the LD competition.

I tried using MuLab for a while, and it seems like a solid piece of music creation software. I ended up using LMMS because it had a better library of sounds and I found more straightforward tutorials for it that allowed me to figure out the program enough to make a simple tune. If you're looking for software to help you make music for your games, I'd recommend looking at those two programs.

Overall, I had a blast participating in Ludum Dare and I feel like a better developer coming out of it. I've been learning Unity and game development for just over 2 years and I'm finally getting to the point where I feel like I know what I'm doing. There were a lot of really cool games submitted this year, too. I've been having a blast playing and rating games the past few days. There are some very creative game ideas out there and it's fascinating to see so many of them in one place.

If you're a game developer looking for a challenge, I highly recommend taking part. The next one is in April and I know I'll be participating! Thanks for reading now get back to work!
